Algebra

 Home Mathematics Area of mathematics
OurBigBook.com Words: 318k Articles: 6k
Algebra studies equations, algebraic operations, and the structures that make their rules work. Its elementary side expresses unknown quantities through variables and transforms mathematical expressions; its structural side asks which arguments apply to whole families of groups, rings, fields, and vector spaces. The useful step is identifying exactly which properties a calculation needs, so that it can be reused in a new setting.
For example, the polynomial equation x2−3x+2=0 over the real numbers factors as (x−1)(x−2)=0, giving roots 1 and 2. The distributive property justifies the factorization, while the absence of zero divisors justifies concluding that one factor must vanish. Over the finite field F2​, the same integer coefficients reduce to x2+x=x(x+1), with roots 0 and 1. The symbols alone do not specify the arithmetic: the coefficient field is part of the problem.
In a ring with zero divisors, a familiar step can fail. Modulo 8, all four residue classes 1,3,5,7 satisfy x2=1. For x=3, the factorization (x−1)(x+1)=2⋅4=0 holds modulo 8, yet neither factor is zero. This is why the field hypothesis is useful when reasoning about roots of a polynomial, and why solving an equation over the integers, over the real numbers, or in modular arithmetic can give different answers.
The structure is also useful beyond scalar arithmetic. Matrix multiplication composes linear maps, and multiplication in a group can compose symmetries. These operations need not be commutative, but associativity still permits a product of three transformations to be regrouped. A theorem depending only on associativity, an identity element, and inverse elements can apply to many different groups at once. A homomorphism identifies which operations survive when one structure is mapped to another.
Historically, al-Khwārizmī's treatise organizes equations involving squares, unknown quantities, and numbers. Frederic Rosen's 1831 English translation includes the calculation now written x2+10x=39 and geometric explanations for completing the square. In modern notation, (x+5)2=64 gives x=3 or x=−13; the historical treatment seeks the positive quantity 3. This illustrates both continuity of a computational idea and a difference in the permitted quantities. [ref]

Substitution (algebra)

Words: 36
Algebra OurBigBook.com
A substitution replaces a variable or subexpression by another expression. In an equation or differential equation, introducing a new variable can expose a simpler form; any division or inverse transformation must retain its domain restrictions and separately check discarded branches.

Abstract algebra

Algebra OurBigBook.com
The study of algebraic structures such as groups, rings and fields through their operations and laws.

Factorization

Words: 25
Algebra OurBigBook.com
Factorization expresses an object as a product of simpler factors. Integer factorization decomposes an integer; polynomial factorization decomposes a polynomial. The permitted factors depend on the ambient algebraic structure.

Rationalizing a denominator

Words: 71
Algebra OurBigBook.com
Multiplying numerator and denominator of a fraction by the same nonzero expression can remove a square root from the denominator. For instance,
a​+b1​=a−b2a​−b​
(1)
when a≥0 and both denominators are nonzero. This uses the difference-of-squares identity (a​+b)(a​−b)=a−b2. If a=b2, the original expression may still be defined even though the rationalized quotient is not, so that case must be handled separately. The related rationalization of a square-root difference applies the same multiplication to a numerator.

Equation (L=R)

Words: 796 Articles: 7
Algebra OurBigBook.com
An equation asserts that two mathematical expressions have the same value. Solving it means finding all allowed assignments to its variables that make that assertion true. It converts a relationship into a constraint: a measurement, a geometric intersection, or an equilibrium model can leave an unknown value to determine.
The allowed values matter. The equation 2x=1 has solution set {1/2} over the rational numbers, but the empty set over the integers. Over the real numbers, x2=1 has two solutions, −1 and 1. A mathematical identity, such as (x+1)2=x2+2x+1, holds for every permitted real x. The familiar equality sign therefore does not by itself say whether one is checking a particular value, solving for an unknown, or stating an identity.
For a worked linear equation over the real numbers,
2x+3=9⟺2x=6⟺x=3.
(2)
The first step subtracts three from both sides; the second divides both sides by the nonzero number two. Reversing the steps recovers the original equation, so these are equivalent equations with the same solution set {3}. Checking the value gives 2⋅3+3=9. The role of reversible operations and the classification by solution sets are described in College Algebra 2e, §2.2: Solving Linear Equations in One Variable.
When the two sides define real-valued functions f and g on a common domain of a function, solutions are exactly the input values at which their function graphs intersect. Equivalently, they are the zeros of a function f−g. This gives a useful connection between symbolic algebra and geometry: rearranging an equation can simplify the comparison without changing the inputs where equality holds.
Not every operation is reversible on every domain of a function. Dividing x(x−1)=0 by x gives x−1=0 only after restricting to x=0; it loses the solution x=0 if that restriction is forgotten. Squaring both sides can instead introduce an extraneous solution, because distinct real numbers can have the same square. The source equation, its domain of a function, and the direction of each implication should travel together.

An equation which is not a linear equation in the specified unknowns.

Unknown (x)

A variable whose value is sought subject to an equation or other constraint.

Implicit equation (F(x,y)=0)

Words: 56
Equation OurBigBook.com
An implicit equation specifies a relation between variables without isolating a designated output as an explicit function of the inputs. For example, x2+y2=1 specifies a circle. On −1<x<1, it determines the two real branches y=±1−x2​, each an implicit function when one branch is selected. The implicit function theorem gives local conditions for a unique differentiable branch; implicit differentiation computes its derivative without first solving explicitly.

System of equations

Words: 51
Equation OurBigBook.com
A system of equations requires one choice of unknowns to satisfy several equations at once. Its solution set is the intersection of the solution sets of the individual equations. For example, x2+y2=1 and y=(x−1)2 ask for intersections of a unit circle and a parabola. A linear system is the special case in which every equation is linear in the unknowns.

Equivalent equations

Words: 94
Equation OurBigBook.com
Two equations are equivalent on a specified domain of a function if they have the same solution set. Adding the same defined mathematical expression to both sides is reversible. Multiplying or dividing both sides by a mathematical expression is reversible only where that expression is nonzero and invertible in the arithmetic being used. In a field, every nonzero scalar is invertible; a general ring needs an additional check.
For example, x2=1 and (x−1)(x+1)=0 are equivalent equations over the real numbers, by the distributive property. Concluding x=1 or x=−1 additionally uses the absence of zero divisors. The modular example in algebra shows why that extra inference can fail in a ring with zero divisors.

Extraneous solution

Words: 177
Equation OurBigBook.com
An extraneous solution satisfies a transformed equation but fails the original equation or its restrictions. The term describes a candidate generated during the calculation, rather than a true solution that can be kept in the final solution set.
Consider the real equation
x​=x−2.
(3)
The square root requires x≥0. Because the square root is nonnegative, any solution must also have x−2≥0, so x≥2. Squaring gives
x=(x−2)2⟺x2−5x+4=0⟺(x−1)(x−4)=0.
(4)
The squared equation has candidates x=1 and x=4. At x=4, the original equality is 2=2. At x=1, it is 1=−1, which fails: this candidate is an extraneous solution. Thus the original solution set is exactly {4}.
On the restricted domain of a function x≥2, both original sides are nonnegative, so squaring is reversible there and the two equations are equivalent. Retaining the sign restriction or checking every candidate in the original equation achieves the same final solution set. The general need to check candidates after raising both sides to a power is explained in College Algebra 2e, §2.6: Solving Radical Equations.

Identity (mathematics)

Words: 90
Equation OurBigBook.com
A mathematical identity is an equation that holds for every assignment in a specified domain of a function. For example, the distributive property gives (x+1)2=x2+2x+1 for every real number x. An identity can replace one mathematical expression by another without imposing a new restriction on that domain.
The domain remains essential. The equality (x2−1)/(x−1)=x+1 holds for every real x=1, but its left side is undefined at x=1. Cancelling a factor does not retrospectively define the original mathematical expression at the excluded input. An identity is different from an identity element of an algebraic operation or an identity function, which are separate concepts despite sharing a name.

Expression (mathematics)

Words: 211 Articles: 1
Algebra OurBigBook.com
A mathematical expression combines symbols according to formation rules, such as 2x+1, (x+1)2, or x​. With values for its variables and meanings for its algebraic operations, it can be evaluated. An equation relates two mathematical expressions; an expression alone need not assert anything.
For example, 2x+3 evaluates to seven at x=2 and nine at x=3. Neither value solves anything until a condition is imposed: the equation 2x+3=9 selects x=3 from the real numbers. This distinction is useful when moving from a formula to a question about which inputs satisfy it. Evaluation by replacing the variables with assigned values is described in College Algebra 2e, §1.1: Evaluating Algebraic Expressions.
Different written mathematical expressions can have the same value for every input in a common domain of a function. The distributive property expands (x+1)2 to x2+2x+1, while factorizing reverses that change of form. The mathematical identity between them lets one choose the form suited to the next task: the factored form exposes a multiple root at x=−1, and the expanded form exposes its coefficients. Simplifying should preserve values on the stated domain, rather than silently enlarging it.

Closed-form expression

Words: 39
Expression (mathematics) OurBigBook.com
A mathematical expression given by a finite combination of specified operations and standard functions, rather than an unevaluated recurrence relation or an unbounded procedure. Which functions are admitted is part of the convention. For example, the sum of the first n positive integers has the closed-form expression n(n+1)/2.

Algebraic K-theory

Algebra OurBigBook.com
Algebraic K-theory studies invariants built from projective modules and their automorphisms over rings. Its lowest groups record the additive projective-module classes and stable invertible matrices, respectively. It differs from Topological K-theory, although vector-bundle clutching and module patching have parallel forms.

A cartesian square of unital rings A=A1​×A0​​A2​ is a Milnor square when at least one map Ai​→A0​ is surjective. Finitely generated projective modules over A can then be assembled from projective modules over the two upper rings together with an isomorphism of their reductions over A0​.

Milnor square OurBigBook.com
Evaluation of the cyclic generator at 1 and at a primitive pth root gives the displayed pullback. The maps to the common field reduce integers modulo p and set ζp​=1. If a representative polynomial for the second component has value c at one, adding an integer multiple of Φp​ adjusts that value by a multiple of p without changing the second component. This proves surjectivity onto compatible pairs.

Mayer-Vietoris sequence in algebraic K-theory (K1​A→K1​A1​⊕K1​A2​→K1​A0​→K0​A→K0​A1​⊕K0​A2​→K0​A0​)

The diagonal maps are extension of scalars; the maps to A0​ are differences. The connecting map sends g to the difference of its patched free module and the corresponding free A-module. Elementary lifting and common free stabilization prove exactness at every internal term. The displayed fragment does not assert injectivity at its first term or surjectivity at its last.

Milnor square OurBigBook.com
A compatible triple (P1​,P2​,ϕ) patches to {(x1​,x2​):ϕ(xˉ1​)=xˉ2​}. It is finitely generated projective and recovers Pi​ after extension of scalars. For free modules glued by g, the block identity diag(g,g−1)∈E∞​(A0​) lifts through the surjective side and makes the direct sum with inverse gluing free. Complements reduce general projective triples to that free case. Conversely an idempotent over A is exactly a compatible pair of idempotents over its two factors.

Algebraic K-theory OurBigBook.com
Stable invertible matrices, with stabilization g↦diag(g,1), form the stable general linear group. Its elementary subgroup is its commutator subgroup, and the displayed quotient is its abelianization. Elementary matrices lift along any surjective ring map, even when arbitrary invertible matrices do not lift. Over a field, determinant identifies K1​ with its multiplicative unit group.

The union of finite invertible matrices under g↦diag(g,1). Every element and relation occurs in a finite matrix size; adding identity blocks permits comparisons between different sizes without changing the stable class.

Words: 43
Stable general linear group OurBigBook.com
The subgroup generated by elementary transvections in finite matrix sizes, with identity stabilization. A third distinct index expresses each transvection as a commutator; stable block identities show that this subgroup is normal and that its quotient in the stable general linear group is abelian. Thus it is precisely the commutator subgroup.

Words: 56
Algebraic K-theory OurBigBook.com
The Grothendieck group of finitely generated projective right A-modules under direct sum. An element is a formal difference [P]−[Q]. Equality of two positive classes means P⊕T≅Q⊕T for some projective T; adding a complement of T converts this into an isomorphism after a common finite free summand. This stabilization criterion is essential in patching arguments.

Algebraic structure

Words: 617 Articles: 5
Algebra OurBigBook.com
An algebraic structure is a set equipped with specified algebraic operations satisfying selected axioms. An operation's domain is part of the structure: a binary operation on S takes two elements of S and produces another element of S. Groups specify one such operation, rings specify addition and multiplication, and vector spaces specify vector addition and scalar multiplication by a separate field.
Different choices of operations can give the same underlying set different structures. The integers form a group under addition, since every integer has an additive inverse. They do not form a group under multiplication: for example, 2 has no multiplicative inverse among the integers. Even the nonzero integers fail that inverse requirement. In contrast, nonzero rational numbers form a group under multiplication.
Finite multiplication tables make such distinctions visible. Arithmetic modulo 5 gives a field; arithmetic modulo 6 gives a commutative ring with zero divisors. In the former, multiplying by any nonzero element permutes all residue classes. In the latter, multiplying by 2 reaches only 0,2,4, and 2⋅3=0 even though both factors are nonzero.
The goal is to extract reusable properties rather than memorize isolated tables. A homomorphism preserves the specified operations, and an isomorphism shows that two structures have identical operation patterns after relabeling.

Vertex operator algebra (a↦Y(a,z))

Words: 45
Algebraic structure OurBigBook.com
A vertex operator algebra is an integer-graded vector space equipped with a state-field correspondence a↦Y(a,z), a vacuum, translation operator and conformal vector satisfying vacuum, translation, locality and compatibility axioms. It packages the local operator product expansions of a chiral conformal field theory. A string vertex operator is an individual state insertion, rather than this complete algebraic structure.

Incline

Words: 158 Articles: 1
Algebraic structure OurBigBook.com
An incline has two associative commutative operations + and multiplication, with multiplication distributing over addition, idempotent addition and absorption x+xy=x. Neither operation is required here to have an identity. Its natural order is x≤y⟺x+y=y, making addition a join. Multiplication is order-preserving, and products lie below both factors. A finitely generated incline is well-quasi-ordered by its reversed natural order, via the reverse-inclusion well-quasi-ordering of monomial ideals applied to exponent supports.

Finitely generated incline is well-quasi-ordered by reverse absorption (x⪯y⟺x+y=x)

Words: 90
Incline OurBigBook.com
Expand every term in finitely many generators as a finite nonempty sum of monomials, and associate its exponent support with the upward-closed subset of Nr that it generates. The reverse-inclusion well-quasi-ordering of monomial ideals supplies an earlier support upset containing a later one. Every later monomial is then a multiple of an earlier monomial, hence is absorbed by it under a+ab=a. The earlier sum absorbs the later sum. Thus every infinite term sequence has an earlier element preceding a later one in the reverse natural order. Reflexivity, antisymmetry and transitivity follow directly from commutative idempotent addition.

Homomorphism (f:A→B)

Words: 216 Articles: 1
Algebraic structure OurBigBook.com
A homomorphism is a map between algebraic structures preserving their specified operations. For a single binary operation, this means f(a∗b)=f(a)⋆f(b), where the source and target may use different operation symbols. A group homomorphism preserves the group operation; a ring homomorphism preserves addition and multiplication, with the identity convention specified; a module homomorphism preserves addition and scalar multiplication.
Reduction modulo 5 is a ring homomorphism Z→Z/5Z: adding or multiplying first and then reducing gives the same residue as reducing first and then operating. For example, 12⋅14=168≡3(mod5), while the reduced operands give 2⋅4=8≡3(mod5). This lets a complicated integer calculation be projected into simpler finite arithmetic. It also explains why a polynomial equation over the integers imposes necessary modular arithmetic conditions on any integer solution.
A homomorphism can lose information: 0 and 5 have the same image under that reduction. An isomorphism loses none of the structure because it has an operation-preserving inverse. Preservation of the operation, rather than preservation of arbitrary labels or sizes, is the essential condition.

Kernel (algebra, kerf)

Words: 58
Homomorphism OurBigBook.com
A kernel records the information lost by a homomorphism. For a group homomorphism it is the preimage of the identity element, giving the kernel of a group homomorphism; for a ring homomorphism or linear map it is the preimage of zero, giving the kernel of a ring homomorphism or kernel of a linear map. More generally, the relation a∼b⟺f(a)=f(b) records which inputs the homomorphism identifies. In the group case, its equivalence classes are cosets of the group kernel, as explained by fibres of a group homomorphism are cosets of its kernel.

Derivation (differential algebra)

Words: 36
Algebra OurBigBook.com
An algebraic derivation of an algebra over a field is a linear map satisfying the Leibniz rule for its multiplication: D(xy)=D(x)y+xD(y). This definition makes sense even when the multiplication is not associative. A derivation of an algebra uses an associative product; a derivation of a Lie algebra uses the Lie bracket as its product.

Normed algebra ((A,∥⋅∥))

Words: 224 Articles: 3
Algebra OurBigBook.com
A normed algebra is an algebra over a field with a norm satisfying ∥ab∥≤∥a∥∥b∥. Its completion is a Banach algebra, since multiplication extends continuously. Completeness is additional structure, rather than part of the definition of a normed algebra.

Dimension bound for a commutative Euclidean normed algebra (dimR​A≤2)

Words: 83
Normed algebra OurBigBook.com
A finite-dimensional commutative real algebra with a Euclidean multiplicative norm has dimension at most two. Automatic real bilinearity from a multiplicative norm supplies bilinearity if it was not part of the initial description. On its unit sphere, squaring has derivative v↦2xv, injective because there are no zero divisors. The only equal squares are antipodal pairs, so the map induces an injective immersion RPn−1→Sn−1. Compactness and the inverse function theorem make it a diffeomorphism when n≥2. For n≥3, the fundamental groups Z/2 and zero contradict this. The real and complex number algebras attain dimensions one and two.

Automatic real bilinearity from a multiplicative norm (∥xy∥=∥x∥∥y∥)

Words: 64
Normed algebra OurBigBook.com
Suppose a ring has an underlying real normed vector space and its norm is multiplicative, without initially assuming real bilinearity of multiplication. For fixed x, distributivity makes y↦xy additive, while ∥xy−xz∥=∥x∥∥y−z∥ makes it continuous. Additivity gives rational scalar compatibility, and continuity extends it to every real scalar. Apply the same argument in the other variable to obtain a bilinear map. The norm identity also excludes nonzero zero divisors.

Normed algebra OurBigBook.com
A normed division algebra is a nonzero unital normed algebra in which every nonzero element has a two-sided multiplicative inverse. The complex Gelfand-Mazur theorem forces such an algebra to be C, even when completeness is not initially assumed: embed it in its Banach algebra completion and use nonemptiness of the Banach-algebra spectrum.

Algebra OurBigBook.com
For an additive semigroup D with identity zero, the semigroup algebra k[D] has a k-basis of formal symbols tq, q∈D, and multiplication tqtq′=tq+q′. For D=Z[1/2]≥0​ it is the integral domain ⋃h≥0​k[t1/2h]. Its positive-exponent ideal is a nonzero idempotent ideal, and the strictly ascending chain (t)⊊(t1/2)⊊⋯ shows that the algebra is not a Noetherian ring.

Semiring

Algebra OurBigBook.com
A semiring has a commutative monoid operation (S,+,0) and a monoid operation (S,⋅,1), with multiplication distributing over addition on both sides and 0 absorbing multiplication. Additive inverses are not required. The natural numbers with their usual addition and multiplication are a basic example. Regarding multiplication as composition yields a one-object category with commutative-monoid enrichment.

Algebra OurBigBook.com
The isomorphism theorems relate homomorphisms, their kernels and images, and quotient constructions in algebra. For groups, the first isomorphism theorem identifies a homomorphism's image with the quotient group by its group kernel. Analogous statements include the first isomorphism theorem for rings and the First isomorphism theorem for vector spaces: identifying precisely the inputs with the same output preserves the remaining algebraic structure.

Irreducibly diagonally dominant matrix

Words: 97
Diagonal dominance OurBigBook.com
A complex square matrix is irreducibly diagonally dominant when every row satisfies ∣aii​∣≥∑j=i​∣aij​∣, at least one row is strict, and its nonzero off-diagonal entries define a strongly connected directed graph. Such a matrix is nonsingular. For if Az=0, choose a component of maximum modulus. The row inequality forces every out-neighbour to have that same modulus, unless the maximum is zero. Connectivity propagates this modulus to a strict row, where the row inequality is impossible. Thus the maximum is zero and z=0. This extends nonsingularity of a strictly diagonally dominant matrix to many finite difference matrices with strict dominance only near a boundary.

Quiver OurBigBook.com
The Kronecker quiver has two vertices and two parallel arrows from the first to the second. For a representation with arrows I,N, an endomorphism consists of the same matrix at both vertices and must commute with N. If N is a single Nilpotent Jordan block, this centralizer is k[N], yielding an indecomposable non-brick when the block size exceeds one.

Quiver OurBigBook.com
An acyclic quiver has no oriented cycle. For a finite quiver, this is equivalent to finite-dimensionality of its path algebra: paths have bounded length without cycles, while powers of a cycle are infinitely many distinct basis elements.

This quiver has r source vertices, each with one arrow to a common sink. Its path algebra has the vertex idempotents and the arrows as basis. After extracting source kernels from a representation, its remaining arrows identify the source spaces with subspaces of the sink.

Preserving the first three lines forces scalar endomorphisms. Its Tits form of a quiver is zero, so the Ringel form gives one-dimensional self-extensions.

Words: 142 Articles: 1
Three-subspace quiver OurBigBook.com
Every triple of subspaces is a direct sum of one-dimensional membership blocks and two-dimensional three-line blocks. Split off the triple intersection, then the pairwise intersections using projections killing the third subspace. Next split complements to Ui​∩(Uj​+Uℓ​), using projections killing the other two subspaces. The remaining subspaces are pairwise disjoint and each lies in the sum of the other two. Their sum is U1​⊕U2​, with U3​ the graph of an isomorphism U1​→U2​. A graph basis splits this into two-dimensional blocks. A complement to the total span supplies zero-membership blocks. This elementary argument classifies the three-subspace quiver.

Endomorphism (EndC​(X))

Words: 673 Articles: 4
Morphism OurBigBook.com
An endomorphism is a morphism f:X→X: its source and target are the same object, with the same specified structure. For a group it is an operation-preserving group homomorphism back into that group; for a vector space it is a linear endomorphism; for a ring it is a ring endomorphism. A self-map must satisfy the chosen compatibility conditions to qualify. The notation EndC​(X) records the category C in which these conditions are imposed. See Riehl, Category Theory in Context, Definition 1.1.10 and the following paragraph.
An endomorphism can lose information or miss part of its target. On the additive integers, d(k)=2k preserves addition and is injective, but is not surjective: no integer maps to 1. On the vector space R2 over the real numbers, the linear endomorphism P(x,y)=(x,0) loses the second coordinate, so it is neither injective nor surjective. Neither is an automorphism. The same doubling rule becomes a group isomorphism when its target is the additive even integers, as explained under isomorphism.
The finite cyclic group C6​=Z/6Z offers a small example of information loss that can be drawn completely. With addition in modular arithmetic, the endomorphism f2​(k)=2k(mod6) sends the inputs 0,1,2,3,4,5 to 0,2,4,0,2,4. Its image of a group homomorphism is {0,2,4} and its kernel of a group homomorphism is {0,3}. Each reached output has two inputs; the other three outputs are missed.
For an endomorphism of a group or ring with a finite underlying set, injectivity is equivalent to surjectivity by counting; either condition makes it an automorphism. The additive integers example shows why the finiteness assumption matters. A linear endomorphism of a finite-dimensional vector space also has equivalent injectivity and surjectivity, this time by the rank-nullity theorem even when its underlying set is infinite.
Self-maps can be iterated without changing the object: f2=f∘f, f3=f∘f∘f, and so on. Composition in a category and the identity morphism make the endomorphisms of a fixed object in a locally small category into a monoid. This packages repeated compatible operations, including irreversible ones, into a single structure.
The general language has a documented historical milestone in the 1945 paper of Samuel Eilenberg and Saunders Mac Lane. They defined categories of objects and compatible maps, and distinguished maps admitting inverses within that category. Their examples included groups, vector spaces, and topological spaces. This gave a common framework for compatible self-maps and their invertible cases. See Eilenberg and Mac Lane, General Theory of Natural Equivalences, pp. 234 and 237–239.

kerfa​={0,n/d,2n/d,…,(d−1)n/d},∣kerfa​∣=d.

In that case a modular inverse b of a gives fa−1​=fb​. This connects reversible self-maps directly to the generators of a finite cyclic group.[ref]

Morphism OurBigBook.com
An automorphism is an isomorphism f:X→X: a structure-preserving self-map that can be undone by another structure-preserving self-map. Equivalently, it is an invertible endomorphism. Its inverse satisfies
f−1∘f=f∘f−1=1X​,
(6)
where 1X​ is the identity morphism. Both maps must be morphisms in the chosen category. For ordinary groups, rings, and vector spaces over a fixed field, a bijective morphism automatically has a compatible inverse. For topological spaces, an automorphism is a homeomorphism from the space to itself: a continuous bijection needs a continuous inverse as well. See Riehl, Category Theory in Context, Definition 1.1.10 and Example 1.1.11.
For example, T(x,y)=(x+y,y) is an automorphism of the vector space R2 over the real numbers, with inverse T−1(u,v)=(u−v,v). Both are linear maps. The linear endomorphism P(x,y)=(x,0) from endomorphism preserves addition and scalar multiplication too, but discards a coordinate and cannot be undone. Preserving the structure and preserving enough information for reversal are separate requirements.
The automorphisms of a fixed object in a locally small category form a group under composition in a category: the identity morphism is the identity element, and the inverse element of a composite reverses the order of its factors. This makes reversible internal changes calculable. For a group, the resulting automorphism group records which relabelings preserve all products; the examples in group automorphism show how restrictive that condition can be.

Group automorphism (α:G∼​G)

Automorphism OurBigBook.com
A group automorphism is a bijective group homomorphism α:G→G. It preserves the group operation, the identity element, and inverse elements; its inverse is another group homomorphism. Thus it is a group isomorphism with identical source and target. These maps form the automorphism group Aut(G) under function composition.[ref]
For the additive finite cyclic group C6​, take f5​(k)=5k(mod6). Its output list on 0,1,2,3,4,5 is 0,5,4,3,2,1, a permutation of all six elements. It preserves addition because 5(a+b)=5a+5b(mod6), and applying it twice gives 25k=k(mod6). Hence it is a group automorphism and its own inverse function. Compare the collapsing f2​ in the figure under endomorphism. The general criterion under endomorphism of a finite cyclic group says exactly when such a map is reversible: its multiplier must be coprime to the size of the finite cyclic group.
A permutation need not be a group automorphism, even if it fixes the identity element. Let π exchange 1 and 2 in C6​ and fix 0,3,4,5. It is a bijection, and π(0)=0, but
π(1+1)=π(2)=1,π(1)+π(1)=2+2=4(mod6).
(7)
Thus it fails to preserve addition and is not even a group homomorphism. Reversibility alone does not preserve the group operation.
A group automorphism carries each cyclic subgroup onto the cyclic subgroup generated by the image of its defining element, preserving the order of a group element. In particular, it carries a generator of a group to another generator of a group. For C6​, the existing calculation of generators of a finite cyclic group leaves only the images 1 and 5 for 1, so its automorphism group consists exactly of the identity function and f5​. This turns the problem of compatible relabeling into a much smaller choice than enumerating arbitrary permutations.

Isomorphism

Morphism OurBigBook.com
An isomorphism is a morphism with a two-sided inverse that is also a morphism. Two objects are isomorphic when such a map exists between them. For groups, rings, and vector spaces, a bijective structure-preserving map has a structure-preserving inverse; in other settings the inverse condition needs separate attention, as for a homeomorphism between topological spaces.
For example, f(k)=2k is a group isomorphism from the additive integers to the additive even integers. It is bijective onto that target, satisfies f(a+b)=f(a)+f(b), and has inverse 2k↦k. The two groups have the same addition pattern even though they are different sets. It is not a ring isomorphism for their inherited multiplications, since f(ab)=2ab while f(a)f(b)=4ab.

Group isomorphism (φ:G∼​H)

Words: 228
Isomorphism OurBigBook.com
A group isomorphism is a bijective group homomorphism φ:G→H. It matches the entire group operation: φ(ab)=φ(a)φ(b), with each product taken in its own group. Its inverse is automatically a group homomorphism. A group automorphism is the special case H=G.[ref]
The target is part of the claim. The doubling example under isomorphism is a group isomorphism d:Z→2Z, between the additive integers and the additive even integers. Exactly the same rule d(k)=2k, declared as d:Z→Z, is an injective endomorphism that misses 1 and every other odd integer, so is not a group automorphism. Changing the declared target changes surjectivity, even though it does not change the formula or its compatibility with addition.
An isomorphism lets a calculation in one model solve the same problem in another. The example under group identifies addition modulo four with function composition of rotations of a square via k↦rk. Through this group isomorphism, adding exponents corresponds exactly to composing motions. More generally, a group isomorphism preserves order of a group element, carries subgroups to subgroups, and carries a generating set of a group to a generating set of a group. Having equally many elements is insufficient: the permutation in group automorphism already fails compatibility on two inputs.
Why does the inverse preserve the group operation? Write u=φ(a) and v=φ(b), possible because of surjectivity. Then
φ−1(uv)=φ−1(φ(a)φ(b))=φ−1(φ(ab))=ab=φ−1(u)φ−1(v).
(8)
This proves the inverse condition directly. Analogous calculations work for each operation of a ring and for addition and scalar multiplication in a vector space. The argument relies on preserving those operations; it supplies no general continuity claim for the inverse of a continuous bijection between topological spaces.

Algebra OurBigBook.com
A field is a commutative ring with 0=1 in which every nonzero element has a multiplicative inverse. Examples include the rational numbers, real numbers, and complex numbers. The integers are a ring but not a field: dividing 1 by 2 leaves them. For a prime number p, the prime field Fp​=Z/pZ is a finite example, because every nonzero residue is coprime to p and hence has a modular inverse.
In F5​, the nonzero inverse pairs are 1−1=1, 2−1=3, 3−1=2, and 4−1=4. Thus 2x=3 has solution x=3⋅3=4 in this field; the real number solution would be 3/2. Dividing by a nonzero coefficient is valid in both settings, but it means division according to the chosen field's operations.
A field has no zero divisors: if ab=0 and a=0, multiplying by a−1 gives b=0. This short argument supports polynomial factorization arguments and pivot division in Gaussian elimination. It does not hold in every commutative ring: modulo 6, the nonzero residues 2 and 3 multiply to zero. The distinction is visible in the figure under algebraic structure.

Field of algebraic numbers (Q​)

Words: 125
Algebraic number OurBigBook.com
The complex algebraic numbers form a field, the algebraic closure of Q inside C. To see closure under the field operations, if α,β are algebraic numbers, the tower law makes Q(α,β) a finite-dimensional field extension of Q. Every element of this extension is an algebraic element, because its successive powers are linearly dependent. In particular it contains α±β, αβ and α/β when β=0.
It is an infinite-degree algebraic extension. A primitive pth root of unity has minimal polynomial of an algebraic element 1+X+⋯+Xp−1 of degree p−1 for every prime p, so the degrees of its finite subextensions are unbounded. Finally a complex root of a polynomial whose coefficients are algebraic numbers is itself algebraic over their finite-degree coefficient field and hence over Q, again by the tower law. Thus every such polynomial splits in this field, establishing the algebraic closure assertion.

Bézout's identity (gcd(a,b)=ax+by)

Words: 115 Articles: 1
Algebra OurBigBook.com
For integers a,b not both zero, there are integers x,y such that ax+by=gcd(a,b). The extended Euclidean algorithm constructs them. For example, 4⋅252−5⋅198=18 and 7⋅5−2⋅17=1; the second identity also gives the modular inverse of 5 modulo 17.
The identity converts a greatest common divisor into a solvability certificate. The linear Diophantine equation ax+by=c is solvable in integers precisely when gcd(a,b) divides c. Every common divisor divides any integer linear combination; conversely, multiplying a Bézout identity by c/gcd(a,b) constructs a solution when that quotient is integral. The coefficients generally are not unique, as the description of all solutions of a linear Diophantine equation makes explicit.

A simple field extension is a field extension generated by one element: F(α) is the smallest subfield of an ambient field containing F and α. Its elements are rational expressions in α with coefficients in F and nonzero denominators. If α is algebraic, its minimal polynomial mα​ identifies F(α)≅F[t]/(mα​), so [F(α):F]=degmα​. In particular, α2∈F but α∈/F implies [F(α):F]=2. Conversely, in characteristic different from two, any degree-two extension is of this form: for β∈/F, express β2=a+bβ in the basis 1,β, then α=β−b/2 has α2=a+b2/4∈F and generates the same extension. Algebraic independence OurBigBook.com
There is a sequence of real numbers for which every finite initial segment consists of algebraically independent elements over the rationals. Given an independent initial segment, specialize each nonzero integer polynomial in one extra variable at those values. At least one coefficient remains nonzero, so each resulting polynomial has finitely many roots. There are countably many such polynomials by countability of integer polynomial rings. Choosing the next real outside the countable union of their roots continues the construction. Clearing denominators makes independence over the integers equivalent to independence over the rationals.

Existence of transcendence bases

Transcendence basis OurBigBook.com
Apply Zorn's lemma to subsets of a field extension with algebraic independence, ordered by inclusion. The union of a chain is independent because any polynomial relation involves only finitely many distinct elements, all of which lie in one member of the chain. A maximal independent set B is a transcendence basis: if any element were transcendental over K(B), adjoining it would preserve independence, by clearing denominators, contradicting maximality. Tuple entries must be distinct in the set-based independence definition; otherwise the nonzero polynomial X1​−X2​ vanishes on a repeated pair and excludes every nonempty set.

Fixed field of inversion in a rational function field (k(t)t↦1/t=k(t+1/t))
Words: 144
Rational function field OurBigBook.com
Let t be transcendental over a field k and let τ be the field automorphism sending t to 1/t. The rational function u=t+1/t is fixed, and t satisfies X2−uX+1=0. Thus the extension over k(u) has degree at most two. It is not one because the nontrivial automorphism τ fixes k(u). The fixed field of τ also has index two by the fixed-field theorem, so it equals k(u).
No nonconstant polynomial in k[t] is fixed by inversion. For a polynomial of positive degree, substitution of 1/t creates negative powers, whereas the original has positive powers. Uniqueness of the coefficients of a Laurent polynomial rules out equality. Consequently this fixed field cannot have a generator that is a polynomial in the original variable, even though it has the simple rational-function generator above. The statement is valid in characteristic two as well: t and 1/t remain distinct transcendental rational functions.

Finite field (Fq​)

Words: 2k Articles: 24
Algebra OurBigBook.com
A finite field is a field with finitely many elements: addition, subtraction, multiplication, and division by a nonzero element all stay inside a finite collection. Write Fq​, or GF(q), for a finite field with q elements. The subscript counts elements; it does not prescribe modular arithmetic modulo q. The field with four elements is the smallest example where that distinction matters.
Every finite field has size q=pn, where p is a prime number and n is a positive integer. To see the counting mechanism, use its prime field Fp​: the finite field is a finite-dimensional vector space over Fp​. For a basis e1​,…,en​, every element has exactly one expression
c1​e1​+⋯+cn​en​,ci​∈Fp​.
(15)
Each coefficient has p choices, so there are pn expressions. Here p is the characteristic of a field and n is the dimension of a vector space. Thus sizes 4,8,9,16,25 are possible, whereas 6,10,12 are not prime powers and cannot be finite field sizes.
Conversely, every prime power occurs, and any two finite fields of the same size admit a field isomorphism. These are classification statements, beyond the counting argument. See Conrad's Theorems 1.5, 2.2, and 2.7.[ref] Uniqueness means the arithmetic agrees after relabeling; it does not choose a basis, an irreducible polynomial for a quotient ring representation, or a particular field isomorphism. Even for the field with four elements, exchanging α and α+1 preserves the arithmetic.
The appeal for coding theory is exact, finite arithmetic with reliable division: polynomial interpolation and linear algebra work over a finite alphabet. A Reed-Solomon code represents messages by polynomials and adds redundancy by evaluating them at several distinct finite field elements. Forney's MIT notes develop this arithmetic as preparation for such error-correcting codes.[ref] In cryptography, finite fields likewise supply exact arithmetic on finitely many symbols, with operations that can be implemented using bits.
Historically, Évariste Galois published work on finite fields beyond prime fields in 1830, constructing them by adjoining elements satisfying irreducible polynomials over prime fields. Conrad's historical account also records E. H. Moore's 1893 terminology, from which the name Galois field and notation GF(q) descend.[ref]

Finite field OurBigBook.com
A finite field has positive characteristic, because its repeated sums of 1 cannot all be distinct. By the characteristic of an integral domain theorem, this is a prime number p. Its multiples of 1 form a copy of the prime field Fp​: a nonzero multiple a1 has inverse b1, where the Bezout identity ab+cp=1 supplies b.
View F as a vector space over this prime field. Repeatedly extend a linearly independent set until it is maximal; the procedure terminates because F is finite. Maximality makes it a basis. If the dimension is d, unique coordinates give exactly pd elements. Thus the cardinality is a power of a single prime, rather than an arbitrary composite integer.

Finite field OurBigBook.com
For a finite field with q elements, exactly q+1 functions from the field to itself preserve multiplication, without requiring additivity or preservation of the identity. They are the constant-zero map, the constant-one map, and the q−1 power maps x↦xk for 1≤k≤q−1.
To prove completeness, f(1)2=f(1) forces f(1)∈{0,1} because a field has no zero divisors. The zero choice forces the constant-zero map. For f(1)=1, nonzero elements must map to nonzero elements, and the restriction is a group homomorphism of the cyclic multiplicative group of a finite field. Its generator has q−1 possible images, giving the q−1 power maps on nonzero elements. Setting f(0)=0 extends each. The only further possibility is f(0)=1, which forces every value to be one. For q=5, this gives six maps. These are generally not field homomorphisms, because preservation of addition was never required.

Field with four elements (F4​)

Words: 344
Finite field OurBigBook.com
Build this finite field by taking a quotient ring of a polynomial ring:
F4​=F2​[t]/(t2+t+1),α=[t].
(16)
The polynomial f(t)=t2+t+1 has f(0)=f(1)=1 in the prime field F2​. A polynomial of polynomial degree two is an irreducible polynomial exactly when it has no polynomial root in the coefficient field. Thus the quotient by an irreducible polynomial is a field construction applies. Its elements have unique representatives a+bα, with a,b∈F2​: precisely 0,1,α,α+1.
The defining relation is α2+α+1=0. Since this finite field has characteristic two, every element equals its additive inverse, and the relation becomes α2=α+1. Addition acts separately on the two coefficients:
(a+bα)+(c+dα)=(a+c)+(b+d)α.
(17)
All coefficient calculations use modular arithmetic modulo two. For example, (α+1)+α=1 and (α+1)+(α+1)=0. Encoding a+bα as the pair of bits (b,a) gives 0↔00, 1↔01, α↔10, and α+1↔11; addition is bitwise exclusive or. These are coordinates in the basis 1,α, so the label 10 does not make α the element 1+1.
For multiplication, expand using the distributive property and replace every α2 by α+1:
(a+bα)(c+dα)=(ac+bd)+(ad+bc+bd)α.
(18)
For example, α(α+1)=α2+α=1, while (α+1)2=α2+1=α. The following complete tables are computed from the coefficient rules. Colors identify results, rather than their numerical sizes. Every row of the addition table lists all four elements, and every nonzero row of the multiplication table does too: adding an element, or multiplying by a nonzero element, can be undone.
The nonzero multiplicative inverses are 1−1=1, α−1=α+1, and (α+1)−1=α. Consequently the equation αx=α+1 has the unique solution x=(α+1)2=α. Repeated multiplication gives α0=1, α1=α, α2=α+1, and α3=1. They cycle through every element of the multiplicative group of a finite field.
Compare the ring Z/4Z, also with four elements. Its addition satisfies 1+1=2=0, and its multiplication satisfies 22=0. Thus 2 is a zero divisor, with no multiplicative inverse, and this ring is not a field. Multiplying by 2 collapses different inputs to the same output: both 0 and 2 give 0, while both 1 and 3 give 2. In the field with four elements, multiplying by α instead rotates the three nonzero elements, preserving their distinctness. The figure makes visible why counting four elements alone does not specify their arithmetic.

The multiplicative group of a finite field Fq​ is the group Fq×​ of its q−1 nonzero elements under multiplication. Zero is excluded because it has no multiplicative inverse. In the field with four elements, these elements are 1,α,α+1, obtained by repeated multiplication by α: they form a cyclic group of group order three. Its addition behaves differently: every nonzero element added to itself gives zero. Keeping the two operations distinct prevents confusing the size of the finite field with the group order of its multiplicative group of a finite field.

A primitive element of Fq​ generates its multiplicative group. This implies Fq​=Fp​(α), but an element generating the field extension need not generate the multiplicative group. For instance u∈F3​[u]/(u2+1) generates the quadratic extension but has order four, whereas 1+u has order eight and is multiplicatively primitive.
Primitive polynomial over a finite field (ord(α)=qm−1)
Words: 65
Primitive element of a finite field OurBigBook.com
A monic polynomial of degree m over Fq​ that is an irreducible polynomial is primitive in the finite-field sense when one of its roots generates the multiplicative group of a finite field Fqm×​. All its roots are Frobenius conjugates and then have the same order qm−1. This notion differs from a primitive polynomial over an integral domain, which concerns the common divisor of its coefficients. Primitive finite-field polynomials provide explicit field representations and primitive cyclic Reed-Solomon codes or BCH codes.

The nonzero elements of every finite field form a cyclic group. For a field with q elements, combine elements realizing each prime-power factor of the group exponent to obtain an element of exponent order; the root bound for Xm−1 then forces that order to be q−1.

Every finite subgroup H of the multiplicative group of a field is cyclic. If m is the exponent of H, commutativity lets one combine elements whose orders realize the prime-power factors of m, producing an element of order m. Every element of H is a root of Xm−1, so the Lagrange root bound over a field gives ∣H∣≤m. Since m≤∣H∣, equality holds and that element generates H.

Injective function OurBigBook.com
Map each real into (0,1) by a fixed bijection, choose its canonical binary expansion, and alternate the two bit sequences as ternary digits 0 and 2. If two such outputs first differ at position k, the leading difference has size 2⋅3−k and the remaining tail has size at most 3−k, so they are unequal. This gives an explicit injection pairing two reals. Iteration encodes every fixed finite real tuple without invoking ambiguous decimal expansions.

At a first differing position, the leading difference exceeds the sum of all possible tail differences, so this is an injection from real sequences to a bounded real interval. The bijection j(n,k)=(n+k−2)(n+k−1)/2+n lists successive finite diagonals.

Irrational number OurBigBook.com
If 2​=p/q in lowest terms, then p2=2q2 makes p even. Substituting p=2r then makes q even, contradicting that the integers are coprime. More quantitatively, ∣2q2−p2∣≥1 for every nonzero integer q, and factoring the difference of squares gives ∣2​−p/q∣≥1/(4q2). To verify the constant, for p/q∈[1,2] the other factor 2​+p/q is less than four; outside this interval the approximation error is at least 2​−1>1/4.

Every nonempty open real interval contains an irrational number. Choose a rational number q strictly inside the interval using density of the rational numbers; then q+2​/N remains inside for sufficiently large positive integers N and is irrational. Thus the irrational numbers form a dense subset of the real line. Together with rational density, this gives approaching sequences of both types at every real point, useful for testing continuity of functions defined differently on the two sets.

Strict descent of powers of a nonzero proper ideal in a Noetherian domain (In⊋In+1)

Words: 111
Noetherian ring OurBigBook.com
Let R be a Noetherian ring that is an integral domain, and let I be a nonzero proper ideal. If In=In+1 for some n≥1, the nonzero finitely generated module M=In satisfies M=IM. Choose generators u1​,…,ur​ and write ui​=∑j​aij​uj​ with aij​∈I. The adjugate matrix identity implies that det(Idr​−(aij​)) annihilates M. This determinant is 1−b for some b∈I, since every term except the constant term contains an entry from I.
The determinant trick has thus supplied (1−b)M=0. A nonzero element of M and multiplicative cancellation in an integral domain force b=1, contradicting properness of I. Therefore all positive powers of an ideal are distinct in this setting. Since they have the same radical of an ideal, there are infinitely many ideals with radical I​.

For a ring homomorphism that is not surjective, apply the same argument with its image as codomain.

Let f∈Cn+1[a,b], n≥1, and let pn​ be its Lagrange interpolation polynomial at ordered distinct interpolation nodes x0​<⋯<xn​. Since f−pn​ vanishes at every interpolation node, Rolle's theorem supplies distinct ηi​∈(xi−1​,xi​) where f′(ηi​)=pn′​(ηi​). The polynomial pn′​ has polynomial degree at most n−1, so it is the interpolation polynomial for f′ at these n new interpolation nodes. Its polynomial interpolation error is the displayed formula, with ξ∈(a,b) depending on x.
Consequently ∣f′(x)−pn′​(x)∣≤M∏i​∣x−ηi​∣/n!≤M(b−a)n/n!, where M=max∣f(n+1)∣. The existence of the interpolation nodes is enough for this bound; their explicit locations generally depend on f. This proof avoids differentiating an unspecified intermediate point in the original polynomial interpolation error formula.

Words: 143
Hermite interpolation OurBigBook.com
Let x0​<⋯<xn​ be distinct interpolation nodes, let f∈C2n+2[x0​,xn​], and let H be the Hermite interpolating polynomial matching the values and first derivatives of f at all nodes. For each x in the interval there is an interior point ξ for which the displayed formula holds. At a node the formula is immediate. Otherwise put e=f−H, π(t)=∏i​(t−xi​) and φ(t)=e(t)−e(x)π(t)2/π(x)2. This function vanishes at the n+1 nodes and at x, while its derivative vanishes at every node. Rolle's theorem gives n+1 additional zeros of its derivative between successive zeros of φ. Repeating the theorem therefore gives φ(2n+2)(ξ)=0. Since H(2n+2)=0 and (π2)(2n+2)=(2n+2)!, rearrangement yields the formula. The extra point x is a zero of φ, not necessarily of its derivative.
For two nodes a,b, this gives the uniform bound ∥f−H∥∞​≤∥f(4)∥∞​(b−a)4/384, since (x−a)2(b−x)2≤(b−a)4/16. The squared nodal factors encode simultaneous matching of values and derivatives.

Hermite interpolating polynomial (H(xi​)=yi​,H′(xi​)=di​)

Words: 65
Hermite interpolation OurBigBook.com
At distinct interpolation nodes x0​,…,xn​, prescribed values yi​ and first derivatives di​ determine exactly one Hermite interpolating polynomial of polynomial degree at most 2n+1. The homogeneous data force a double root of a polynomial at every interpolation node. Hence the kernel of a linear map given by these 2n+2 conditions is zero: a nonzero polynomial with those double roots of a polynomial would have polynomial degree at least 2n+2. Equal finite dimensions of a vector space then give existence as well as uniqueness. This interpolation polynomial is distinct from the Hermite polynomials forming a classical orthogonal polynomial family.

Recover a plaintext from an RSA cryptosystem ciphertext and the public key, without a supplied private key. Integer factorization of the modulus suffices; the existence of an efficient general reduction in the reverse direction is not known.

RSA cycling attack

RSA cryptosystem OurBigBook.com
Repeatedly apply the public RSA cryptosystem encryption map to a ciphertext. A return to that ciphertext reveals its preceding iterate as the plaintext. A nontrivial greatest common divisor between an iterate-minus-start and the modulus instead enables integer factorization. Eventual return alone supplies no useful running-time bound.

RSA cryptosystem OurBigBook.com
An attack exploiting a known relation between plaintexts encrypted using one textbook RSA cryptosystem key. For public exponent three and a known nonzero additive difference, two cubic equations can yield a linear relation recovering a plaintext. A small unknown difference can be enumerated.

An attack exploiting preservation of an algebraic operation by encryption or signing. The textbook RSA cryptosystem has E(m1​m2​)=E(m1​)E(m2​)(modN), so unprotected ciphertexts can be modified multiplicatively. Authentication must be verified before accepting a modified message.

m≡c1a​c2b​(modN),

using modular inverses for negative exponents.

Knowledge of a valid public and private exponent gives ed−1, a nonzero multiple of λ(N). Writing it as 2st with t odd and testing random bases produces a nontrivial square root of one modulo N with high probability; a greatest common divisor then factors N. Thus one customer's private key under a shared semiprime modulus compromises every exponent using that modulus.

Square root of unity (x2=1)

Words: 56
Root of unity OurBigBook.com
A square root of unity is an element x of a ring with identity satisfying x2=1. In a field of characteristic different from two, the only possibilities are 1 and −1: the difference of squares identity (x−1)(x+1)=0 has no other roots because a field has no zero divisors. In a general ring more solutions may occur; modulo eight the four residue classes 1,3,5,7 all have square one.

Words: 88
Root of unity OurBigBook.com
Let S be a finite multiset of nonzero complex numbers such that taking the m2th powers permutes it for every positive integer m. Taking m=2 and iterating the resulting permutation shows that each z∈S obeys z4r=z for some r≥1, hence is a root of unity. Let d be a common multiple of their orders. The d2th powers are all one, and the assumed permutation then forces every original element to be one. For a unitary matrix, the spectral theorem for normal operators further forces the matrix itself to be the identity.

They form a cyclic group by the finite multiplicative subgroup of a field is cyclic theorem. In particular they have order n when gcd(n,q)=1.

Let M be an m-by-n matrix over a principal ideal domain R. Choose Smith normal form PMQ=D with exactly r nonzero diagonal entries. Two nonzero elements with no common nonunit irreducible factor. In a unique factorization domain this is equivalent to their greatest common divisor being a unit. Every nonzero nonunit in a unique factorization domain is a finite product of irreducible elements. Such a factorization is unique up to permutation and multiplication of the factors by units. Irreducibles are prime elements, so divisibility can be checked by comparing their multiplicities. This applies to a polynomial ring over a field and is useful for intersections of localizations inside its fraction field.

The Nagata theorem for divisor class groups then says that Cl(A) is generated by the height-one primes containing x; the only one is the principal prime (x), so Cl(A)=0.

Fundamental theorem of algebra

Words: 178 Articles: 2
Algebra OurBigBook.com
Every nonconstant complex polynomial has a complex root and therefore factors completely into linear factors over C.

Brownian recurrence proof of the fundamental theorem of algebra

Words: 71
Fundamental theorem of algebra OurBigBook.com
If a nonconstant complex polynomial were zero-free, its reciprocal would be an entire bounded function. The real part of its value along planar Brownian motion is a bounded martingale, hence converges almost surely. If that real part were nonconstant, continuity would give two disks with separated value ranges, and recurrence of planar Brownian motion would force alternate visits to both at arbitrarily large times, contradicting convergence. It is therefore constant; the Cauchy-Riemann equations then make the reciprocal constant, a contradiction.

Brownian proof of the fundamental theorem of algebra

Words: 88
Fundamental theorem of algebra OurBigBook.com
If a nonconstant complex polynomial P had no zeros, its reciprocal g=1/P would be an entire holomorphic function, bounded and tending to zero at infinity. Its real and imaginary parts are harmonic functions. Thus g(z+Bt​), for planar Brownian motion started at zero, is a bounded complex martingale with expectation g(z). For fixed R, the Gaussian density bounds P(∣z+Bt​∣≤R) by R2/(2t). Outside a sufficiently large disk, ∣g∣≤ε. Hence ∣g(z)∣≤ε+∥g∥∞​R2/(2t). Let t→∞ and then ε↓0 to obtain g(z)=0, a contradiction. This proves the fundamental theorem of algebra without the maximum modulus principle.
